deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous page (57) sets out Riemann's 1854 theory of 'Spannungselectricität' in imperfect conductors, with flux xi = rho du/dx + alpha drho/dx and a diffusion-type equation for rho. That is the content of his Göttingen Naturforscherversammlung talk 'Über die Gesetze der Vertheilung von Spannungselectricität in ponderabeln Körpern…' (1854, in the Werke). The next page is a heat-conduction lecture on Duhamel superposition. This page opens a new problem.

1. TITLE (written twice, the second time as a revised heading): 'Determination of the distribution of tension (static) electricity in a ring when a constant electromotive force acts in one cross-section.' This is the free charge on a closed conducting ring carrying a steady current driven by an emf localised in one cross-section, i.e. the Kirchhoff/Weber surface-charge problem for a current-carrying circuit, here for a ring.

2. GENERAL METHOD (German prose, heavily corrected). One usually finds a mass distribution producing given effects by first determining its potential u everywhere. The distribution then follows from the theorem: if m is the mass in a closed region bounded by S, dS a surface element, and du/dp the derivative of u along the normal p (the change of potential divided by an infinitesimal normal displacement dp), then
   ∫_S (∂u/∂p) dS = −4π m.
This is Gauss's flux theorem with p the outward normal and the convention Δu = −4πρ.

3. PROOF SKETCH (partly struck). For a unit mass at a point O, with r the distance from O to dS:
   ∫_S ∂(1/r)/∂p dS = −4π if O lies inside S, and 0 if O lies outside.
Riemann writes 'je nachdem O innerhalb oder ausserhalb S liegt'. The lower entry of his brace is hard to read. Also
   −∫ (∂r/∂p)/r² dS = ∫ cos(r,p)/r² dS,
which is the solid-angle form. The sign depends on whether r is directed from O to dS or the reverse; with r from O, ∂r/∂p = cos(r,p) and an overall minus is needed.

4. LAPLACE EQUATION IN CYLINDRICAL COORDINATES (r, φ, x), with x along the ring's axis of symmetry. Volume element dr · r dφ · dx (he writes dψ for the axial differential). He balances the flux through the faces r dφ dψ and (r+dr) dφ dψ, giving ∂(r ∂u/∂r)/∂r dφ dψ dr, and similarly in φ, ∂(∂u/(r∂φ))/∂φ dφ. The result is
   (1/r) ∂(r ∂u/∂r)/∂r + (1/r²) ∂²u/∂φ² + ∂²u/∂x² = 0.
This is correct.

5. ANSATZ FOR THE RING. 'u + βφ': the potential is split into a multivalued part βφ plus a single-valued part.
   (a) [My completion] φ is harmonic (∂²φ/∂φ² = 0 and φ does not depend on r or x).
   (b) ∇φ is tangent to every surface of revolution about the x-axis, so ∂φ/∂n = 0 on the ring surface.
   (c) Hence inside a homogeneous ring the steady current potential is exactly βφ (plus a constant), with a jump 2πβ equal to the emf across the cut.
   (d) The external potential must be harmonic, vanish at infinity and equal βφ (plus a constant) on the ring surface. The surface charge is −(1/4π) times the jump of the normal derivative.
The next line ('u · ( … ) ββ = αx'?) is an illegible attempt at the resulting equation; I cannot reconstruct it with certainty.

6. SCRATCH INTEGRATIONS (lower half). The pieces are consistent with a partial-fraction integration of dz/(√z (1−z)(1−a² z)) with a = 3/4.
   (a) ∫ dz/(√z(1−z)) = log((1+√z)/(1−√z)).
   (b) ∫ dz/(√z(α²−z)) = (1/α) log((α+√z)/(α−√z)); this matches the transcribed ∂x/√x · 1/(α − x²) and the log((√z−α)/(√z+α)) terms.
   (c) Combined: log((1+√z)/(1−√z)) − (3/4) log((1+¾√z)/(1−¾√z)), written by Riemann with reciprocal arguments (the overall sign is flipped). Its derivative is (1−a²)/(√z(1−z)(1−a²z)).
   (d) Exponentiating gives x = (1+√z)/(1−√z) · ((1−a√z)/(1+a√z))^{3/4}, and a variant (¾+√z)/(¾−√z) · ((1−√z)/(1+√z))^{3/4}.
   (e) A second group treats ∫ (x−β)^{−1/2}(x−α)^{1/2} dx/x. It uses the rationalising combinations √(z+α) ± √(z−α), whose square is 2z + 2√(z²−α²) and whose product is 2α, and assembles a quotient of such expressions.
These are elementary antiderivatives. Their link to the ring problem (perhaps an ODE from separation of variables, perhaps unrelated scratch) cannot be established from the page.
errors: The second value in the brace for ∫∂(1/r)/∂p dS appears to be written as −2π (or similar). For O outside S the correct value is 0; −2π holds only for O on a smooth part of S. Possibly a slip, or the reading is uncertain.
Sign: ∂(1/r)/∂p = −(1/r²)∂r/∂p. With r measured from O to dS, ∂r/∂p = cos(r,p), so −∫(∂r/∂p)/r² dS = −∫cos(r,p)/r² dS. The equality with +∫cos/r² as written needs the opposite orientation of r.
In the transcribed x = (1+√z)/(1−√z)·((1+α√z)/(1+α√z))^{3/4} the inner fraction must be (1−α√z)/(1+α√z) (or its reciprocal), as the log line shows. This is a transcription or writing slip.
The log line carries the opposite overall sign to the integral of 1/(√z(1−z)) (reciprocal arguments). This is harmless if intended as −∫ or as log of 1/x.
The line 'u·(…)ββ = αx' is not a meaningful equation as transcribed. It is an incomplete working step.

results.what: Gauss flux theorem ∫∂u/∂p dS = −4πm used to recover a mass (charge) distribution from its potential
results.modern_name: Gauss's law / divergence theorem for the Newtonian potential

results.what: ∫∂(1/r)/∂n dS = −4π or 0 according as the point is inside or outside S (solid-angle integral)
Laplace equation in cylindrical coordinates derived by a flux balance on a volume element
Formulation of the free (surface) charge on a current-carrying ring with emf in one cross-section; interior potential βφ (multivalued azimuthal potential)
results.modern_name: Surface charges on steady-current conductors (Kirchhoff–Weber problem), toroidal conductor
results.usually_credited_to: Kirchhoff 1849/1857, W. Weber 1852; explicit torus solution in modern literature (e.g. Assis et al. 1999–2007)

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is standard potential theory (Gauss flux theorem, cylindrical Laplacian) plus elementary integrals. The problem posed, static charge on a ring carrying a current driven by a localized emf, links to Riemann's known 1854 work on Spannungselectricität and the Kirchhoff–Weber surface-charge question. The page only sets up the problem (the βφ ansatz) without a solution, so it is a notable but minor unpublished detail.

transcription_corrections: Title (both versions): 'Vertheilung der Spannungselectricität in einem Ringe, wenn in einem Querschnitt eine constante electromotorische Kraft vorhanden ist'. The right-hand heading begins with a struck word ('Vorläufige'?) replaced by something like 'Bestimmung der'.
'durch [-…-] gefunden' likely reads 'wird meistens am leichtesten dadurch gefunden, dass man zuerst das von ihr bewirkte Potential … allenthalben bestimmt'.
'{+Anzahl+} geschlossenen Raume' is more plausibly '{+beliebigen+} geschlossenen Raume'.
The parenthesis reads roughly: '(d. h. eine unendlich kleine Ortsänderung dp senkrecht auf die Oberfläche dividirt in die dadurch bewirkte Aenderung des Potentials)'.
The brace values are '−4π' and a second entry, likely '0' (or a struck −2π); the text says 'je nachdem O innerhalb oder ausserhalb S liegt'.
'dr·r dφ·dψ' is the volume element; ψ denotes the axial coordinate (later written x).
In x = (1+√z)/(1−√z)(…)^{3/4}, the inner fraction is (1−α√z)/(1+α√z) or its reciprocal, not (1+α√z)/(1+α√z).
'∂x/√x · 1/(α−x²)' is better read as ∂z/(√z(α²−z)), consistent with the log((√z−α)/(√z+α)) term.
'z = [?]y²/(z²−α²)' is probably a substitution involving √(z²−α²); the reading is uncertain.
